title: Assessing how wind affects bird migration across the continental United States using a novel wind‐favourability metric
content:
What kinds of wind conditions do migratory birds contend with? We used weather radar data from across the continental United States to determine what general direction migrating birds prefer to fly, and we compared this information with wind data to develop a wind favourability index. We then applied this index to observe where and when favourable winds occur. This image shows that favourable winds (indicated by green) for spring migration occur mainly in the southeastern quadrant of the continent.


Abstract

Across migratory bird species that breed in the northern hemisphere, post-breeding or fall migrations generally appear to be longer in duration than pre-breeding migrations in the spring. One explanation is that birds encounter less favourable winds during fall migration than they do during spring migration. We tested whether winds were more favourable in the spring for migrating birds by combining wind data for the continental United States from 1995 to 2024 with a radar-derived metric for the preferred direction of movement for migratory birds. From these two data sources, we generated a novel index for wind favourability that we could apply across the three major North American flyways. We found evidence for more favourable winds during the spring, especially for the central and eastern flyways, but the western flyway tended to have more favourable winds during the fall. These findings help explain differences in spring and fall migration and highlight the importance of the low-level jet (an air current that flows through the centre of North America) in the aerial habitats of migrating animals. To enable others to use the tools presented here, we provide R code for data compilation and analysis as well as a shiny app that enables users to quickly map and visualize wind favourability.
